subject: Coffee & Tea
title: Darjeeling: The Champagne of Tea
description: A short lesson to help you apply Darjeeling: The Champagne of Tea.

hook.text: Darjeeling tea grows in the foothills of the Himalayas. It's called 'the Champagne of teas' for good reason.

buildup.text: High altitude, misty mornings, and dramatic temperature swings give Darjeeling its unique muscatel grape flavor.

discovery.text: First flush (spring) Darjeeling is light and floral. Second flush (summer) is richer with that famous muscatel note.

twist.text: More 'Darjeeling' is sold worldwide than the region produces. Counterfeiting is rampant.

climax.text: India created the Darjeeling logo—a woman holding a tea leaf—to certify authentic origin.

punchline.text: Himalayan altitude, muscatel flavor, fiercely protected name.

quiz.question: Why is Darjeeling tea called 'the Champagne of tea'?
options: Its unique muscatel flavor from high-altitude growing conditions

details.summary: Darjeeling tea is grown at high altitudes in the Himalayan foothills of West Bengal, India. Often called the champagne of teas, its first flush produces a light, floral, and muscatel character unlike any other Indian tea. Genuine Darjeeling has a protected geographical indication.
details.whyItMatters: Darjeeling proves that India produces far more than robust Assam. Its delicacy rivals the finest Chinese teas and commands premium prices worldwide.
takeaways: Darjeeling grows at 600 to 2,000 meters in the Himalayas
First flush is the most prized for its floral muscatel notes
It has protected geographical indication status

faq.question: What does muscatel mean in Darjeeling tea?
faq.answer: Muscatel describes a distinctive grape-like, musky sweetness unique to premium second flush Darjeeling tea. It is caused by the leafhopper insect's bite, which triggers the plant to produce terpenes. This natural stress response creates the prized muscatel character.

faq.question: How much Darjeeling tea is actually genuine?
faq.answer: Darjeeling gardens produce about 8 to 10 million kilograms annually, but an estimated 40 million kilograms are sold worldwide under the Darjeeling name. Counterfeiting is rampant. The Tea Board of India certifies authentic Darjeeling with a logo, but enforcement remains challenging.
